statement: THD is the ratio of the RMS voltage of the harmonics to that of the fundamental, obtained by measuring each harmonic and RMS-summing them, then dividing by the fundamental and expressing the result in percent.
THD+N is the RMS summation of all output components except the fundamental over a prescribed bandwidth, typically 22 kHz, 30 kHz or 80 kHz, after removing the fundamental with a notch filter.
THD+N is always a larger number than THD because it includes noise and other artifacts in addition to harmonics.
SMPTE IMD uses 60 Hz and 7 kHz tones in a 4:1 amplitude ratio (12 dB) and measures the modulation sidebands on the high tone.
ITU-R (formerly CCIF) IMD uses two equal-amplitude tones spaced 1 kHz apart, commonly 13/14 kHz or 19/20 kHz, and usually only the first two or three intermodulation components are measured.
S/N is measured with no signal but with the input terminated, using an RMS voltmeter and a stated bandwidth; 22 kHz flat is the most common condition.
A-weighting rolls off low frequencies, reducing the second and third line harmonics by about 20 dB and 12 dB, and can improve a noise specification by about 10 dB, hiding hum.
The ITU-R 468 weighting filter correlates better with hearing than A-weighting and adds about 12 dB of gain in the critical midband.
Dynamic range is the ratio of maximum output to the noise floor, with the reference level and noise bandwidth stated.
Crosstalk is measured with one channel driven and the other terminated; capacitive coupling makes it rise at about 6 dB/octave with frequency, so the test frequency must be stated.
Frequency response should be stated as a tolerance, for example 20 Hz to 20 kHz +0/-0.5 dB; a response that rises with frequency indicates instability in solid-state equipment.
CMRR is measured by driving both inputs through two equal, carefully matched resistors of half the expected source resistance, and the test frequency must be stated.
Maximum input level must state balanced or unbalanced and the distortion criterion; the preferred criterion is 1% THD, while 'visible clipping' can be as much as 10% distortion.
Input and output impedance must state balanced or unbalanced and whether the port is floating or ground-referenced.
The IEC view is that THD should not be tested above 6 kHz when measuring five harmonics with a 30 kHz bandwidth, or above 10 kHz when measuring the first three harmonics.
An 80 kHz measurement bandwidth is useful during design and manufacturing to reveal high-frequency artifacts, while 22 kHz flat is a defensible published THD+N condition.
ITU-R BS.1770 specifies algorithms for determining subjective programme loudness and true-peak signal level.
The BS.1770 loudness algorithm uses K-weighting, per-channel mean square, channel-weighted summation with the LFE channel excluded, and 400 ms gating blocks overlapped by 75%.
LKFS means loudness, K-weighted, relative to nominal full scale; a 0 dBFS 997 Hz sine on the left, centre or right channel reads -3.01 LKFS.
In this repository, distortion means non-linear distortion added by active devices, not a linear frequency-response error.
1% distortion is -40 dB, 0.1% is -60 dB, 0.01% is -80 dB, 0.001% is -100 dB, and 0.0001% is -120 dB relative to the signal.
A 40 dB notch cannot measure below 1% distortion, and a 100 dB notch cannot measure below 0.001%, because residual fundamental leaks through the notch.
Measuring below 0.01% THD+N with single-frequency cancellation is difficult because noise often dominates the residual.
A sinewave is used for THD because it has a single known fundamental, so any added components are measurable; a complex signal makes the residual harder to interpret.
A THD or THD+N number without test frequency, level, gain, load and bandwidth is not a specification.
The measurement system's own noise and distortion set the floor; at very low distortion levels the residual is mostly noise.

A full-disclosure THD specification sweeps 20 Hz to 20 kHz at +4 dBu with the fifth harmonic or higher measured; for signal processing the preferred gain is unity, and for microphone preamps maximum gain.

True-peak level is the maximum positive or negative value of the signal waveform in the continuous-time domain, which may be higher than the largest sample value; a peak-sample meter can under-read because peaks occur between samples.

statement: Conventional distortion metrics measure spectral components generated by the device and absent from the input, but nonlinear system analysis shows additional distortion contributions that coincide with the fundamental frequencies and are therefore neglected by conventional metrics.
